stories.title: The Wicked Witch Thought Experiment
stories.description: Tim Urban's thought experiment: if a witch made all material goods disappear but left knowledge intact, how long would it take to rebuild an iPhone 6S? It highlights the difference between theoretical knowledge and the complex web of supply chains and tacit knowledge needed for modern technology.

stories.title: Silphium: The Lost Herb
stories.description: The Romans had a prized herb called Silphium (used as seasoning, perfume, aphrodisiac, and contraceptive) which went extinct. A Turkish scientist recently found a Ferula plant in Turkey/Greece that might be it. Interestingly, the Roman 'poor man's substitute' was Hing (Asafoetida), which is also a Ferula.

stories.title: Dhaka Muslin
stories.description: A legendary fabric from Bengal with a thread count of 1200 (vs 40 today), made from a specific plant on the banks of the Meghna river. The plant and the knowledge (16 villages of specialization) were lost. Scientists recently found a plant with 70% DNA match and a weaver managed to make a 300-count version.

stories.title: Fogbank
stories.description: A classified aerogel material used in US nuclear warheads. When they needed to refurbish warheads after decades, they realized they had lost the 'tacit knowledge' of how to make it despite having documents. They had to spend $70M to reinvent it.

stories.title: The Guard and the Bench
stories.description: A story about a guard standing by a bench for no reason. It turns out the paint was wet decades ago, and the order to guard it was never rescinded, becoming a mindless tradition.

stories.title: Artemisinin
stories.description: Yu Tu, a non-PhD researcher in China during the Vietnam War, rediscovered a malaria cure (Artemisinin) from ancient Chinese texts (using cold extraction of wormwood) after 2000 other plants failed.

stories.title: Post-War Germany and Japan
stories.description: Despite total physical destruction, these nations bounced back quickly because the 'software' (human capital, institutions, property rights) survived, proving that knowledge is more resilient than material goods.

recommendations.comment: Amit mentions Leonard Read's essay, which illustrates how no single person knows how to make a pencil, highlighting the miracle of the market and dispersed knowledge.
Amit mentions Cormac McCarthy's post-apocalyptic novel as a depiction of what would happen if civilization collapsed.
Ajay recommends Stefan Zweig's novella about a man in solitary confinement who plays chess against himself to stay sane.

Amit recommends Ben Goldacre's book (he says 'Bad Medicine' but likely means this or 'Bad Pharma') as a guide to skepticism about medical claims.

recommendations.item: On the Natural History of Destruction
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends W.G. Sebald's book, which combines text and photographs to describe the devastation of German cities in WWII.
Amit recommends Pallavi Aiyar's travelogue on Japan.
Ajay recommends Isaac Asimov's short story about a civilization that experiences darkness only once every few thousand years.

core_ideas.description: Knowledge is not just a 'coastal shelf' that accumulates; it can be washed away. We must actively preserve it, as shown by the loss of Silphium and Dhaka Muslin.
Documents aren't enough. The 'Fogbank' story shows that without the people and the tacit knowledge (the 'how-to' that isn't written down), you can't recreate complex things.
Rebuilding civilization isn't just about engineering ('hardware'); it's about 'social technology' like prices, markets, and institutions ('software').
Tradition (ancient texts) contains nuggets of truth found by trial and error (like Artemisinin) but is mostly 'rubbish' (2000 failures). Science is the tool to filter the truth from the noise.
Quackery persists due to reversion to the mean, confirmation bias, and the powerful placebo effect. Scientific trials must beat the placebo, not just 'doing nothing'.
